Same *shape* — consume the frozen CLI contract, emit the platform's native result format — is not the same *outcome*. Collapsing any two would discard one platform's spec entirely.

### #531 does not silently re-own any adapter's acceptance criteria — checked explicitly

This was the specific risk flagged for this pass, and it does not materialize. #531 owns only what no single adapter can own: the one shared lab and 300-submission fixture corpus, the golden per-student score vectors, `CrossPlatformScoreParityTest` comparing all four outputs byte for byte, hermetic containerized execution with **no platform account or network dependency**, two-consecutive-run byte determinism, and hosting the conformance ordering so a seeded #524 contract violation fails the build *before any adapter test executes*.

The relationship runs the other way from re-ownership: each adapter carries its own "byte-identical to the other adapters' score vectors from the same xUnit input" clause explicitly marked **"(feeds CAP-21 AC-1)"** — the adapters supply the inputs, #531 performs the comparison. Rule 3(b): a shared prerequisite (the frozen contract of #524) and a shared consumer (#531), not a shared outcome. Nothing in #531 specifies `results.json` emission, check annotations, `externalGrader` payloads, or notebook cells.

**One consistency obligation, recorded rather than merged:** #531's fixture is the *single* source of the lab and the 300-submission corpus. Boundary note: #533 / #535 (feature deduplication, pass 1)

Checked as a duplicate pair — both re-render the canvas at a chosen simulation time, so they read as two spellings of "show me the circuit at time T". **Not duplicates; no merge.** The boundary:

- **#533 (PF-4) — forward, one event at a time, animated.** A stepping mode advances the simulation by **exactly one event**, and by **one wavefront** (all events at the current timestamp), on demand; each step animates the affected wires, highlights the producing and consuming elements, and shows simulated time advancing by the stepped delay. Per-gate delay stops being a number in a dialog and becomes time a student watches pass. Its gate is that stepping the hazard demo reproduces the **same final state and event sequence** as free-running simulation (same-time ordering determinism pinned by existing goldens), and that batch/headless output is byte-identical with the feature present. It is interactive-only, adds no new state, and never moves backwards.
- **#535 (PF-6) — backward, to an arbitrary T, by re-simulation.** Dragging the cursor to an earlier time $T$ redisplays canvas state at $T$, implemented as **deterministic re-simulation truncated at $T$** and explicitly **never** as per-element checkpoint machinery (#498 §8 exclusion 2 stays untouched; FEAT-035 #363 is deliberately not a dependency). Replay is $O(T)$ with honest progress display rather than a pretended seek. Its gate is `RewindEqualsReplayTest`: for randomized fixtures and times $T$, displayed state after rewind is byte-identical to a fresh run truncated at $T$.

Different directions, different mechanisms, different failure modes: #533's risk is that stepping perturbs same-time event ordering; #535's risk is that replay is not deterministic at all — and KC-23-3 says that if it is not, the response is to **stop and file the determinism finding** rather than paper over it with snapshots. Neither test substitutes for the other, and neither feature's mechanism produces the other's outcome: single-event animation cannot reach an arbitrary earlier $T$, and truncated re-simulation shows no wavefront.

`ordering_after` records the asymmetry: #533 is `[]` (independent), #535 is `[FEAT-C23-1]`. Also relevant to a later pass on #535: the August 2026 product review (#508) recommends **cutting #535's viewer-sync half**, which does not touch the rewind half and does not touch #533 at all.

5226987749.body:
## Absorbing #727 (feature/task deduplication)

**The survivor is a `tier:feature`; the absorbed issue is a `tier:task`. Note the tier consequence — see the last section.**

#727 (TASK-C541-1) is the only task filed against this feature, and its outcome **is** this feature's whole outcome, not a slice of it. Titles are near-verbatim — this issue: *"one command exports the whole handout figure set — schematic, TikZ, timing figure, animation — from one circuit and one recorded run"*; #727: *"one command over one circuit and one recorded run emits the whole handout figure set, and the figures cannot disagree with each other"*. Its acceptance criteria 1–4 restate this issue's AC-1–AC-4 almost word for word, including the same `HandoutBundleTest` / CAP-24 AC-1 pin and the same in-tree LaTeX document building clean in CI. Lower number wins: **#541 survives, #727 closes into it.**

This is the rule-3 near-verbatim case, not the intended feature→task hierarchy. A task that implements *part* of a feature is a slice and stays; #727 implements the feature entire, so keeping both means the same one-command bundle contract is owned twice.

Everything below is scope or an edge #727 carried that this issue's body does not. **After #727 closes, this comment is the only record of it.**

---

### A. Acceptance criteria #727 stated more strictly — adopt these readings

1. **AC-2 gains a refusal clause.** This issue's AC-2 reads *"The command takes exactly one circuit and one recorded-run artifact as input"* — a statement of the input arity, with no stated behaviour when it is violated. #727's AC-2: *"The command accepts exactly one circuit and one recorded-run artifact; **supplying a second run, or none, is refused by name rather than defaulted**."* This is the load-bearing half. The failure mode this feature exists to make impossible (figures that disagree with each other or with the run, CAP-24 risk 4) returns immediately if a second run is silently accepted or a missing one silently defaulted — a bundle that quietly picks a run is exactly a bundle whose figures can disagree. Refusal must name what it refused.

2. **AC-3's deterministic set includes PDF.** This issue's AC-3 lists *"(SVG, TikZ, WaveJSON)"* as the artifacts that must reproduce byte-identically on a re-run over the same inputs. #727's AC-3 lists **`(SVG, PDF, TikZ, WaveJSON)`**. PDF belongs in the set: #536 (TASK-C536-3, #711) already owns *"PDF comes out of the same deterministic renderer, not out of an SVG converter — and both outputs are byte-identical on all three platforms"*, so a bundle that excludes PDF from its own determinism criterion is weaker than the artifact it composes. The animation is correctly excluded from the byte-identical set in both bodies (it is the one artifact whose determinism obligation lives with #539's encoder).

3. **AC-5, which this issue has no equivalent of: the bundle layout is documented in-tree.** #727 requires the directory layout be written down in the repository, not left implicit in the test. Without it, "the bundle" is defined only by whatever `HandoutBundleTest` happens to assert, and an instructor consuming the output from a course repo has nothing to read.

4. **The PF-4 cut becomes an acceptance criterion rather than a note.** This issue carries the #508/#505 REPLAN contingency in its *"Boundary and reference notes"*. #727 promotes it into AC-5: if #508's recommendation to cut PF-4 animation is adopted by REPLAN on #505, the animation drops from the contract **by that same REPLAN rather than by silent omission**. The phrasing matters — it forbids an executor from quietly shipping four artifact kinds and calling the bundle complete.

---

### B. The task-level ordering edges, which this issue only had at feature level

This issue declares `ordering_after: [FEAT-C24-1, FEAT-C24-2, FEAT-C24-3, FEAT-C24-4]` — symbolic feature ids. #727 resolved them to the concrete producing **tasks**, which is the form an executor can actually check:

```yaml
ordering_after: [TASK-C536-3, TASK-C537-2, TASK-C538-2, TASK-C539-2]
```

Resolved to issue numbers:

| #727's edge | Issue | What it produces that the bundle consumes |
|---|---|---|
| TASK-C536-3 | **#711** | print-styled SVG **and** PDF from one deterministic renderer, byte-identical on all three platforms |
| TASK-C537-2 | **#714** | the CircuiTikZ approximation table and the in-tree LaTeX sample document that builds in CI |
| TASK-C538-2 | **#718** | the headless VCD → WaveJSON path checked against a rendered golden SVG |
| TASK-C539-2 | **#722** | the N-cycle animation over a selected canvas region, from a recorded run and no other source |

Note these are the *last* task of each producing feature, not the first — the bundle needs each artifact kind finished, including #711's PDF leg and #714's CI-built sample document. `band_mw: 1-2` is unchanged from this issue.

---

### C. What does **not** change, recorded so the merge is not read as scope creep

- **This issue stays composition-only.** Its own boundary note — *"each artifact kind is owned by FEAT-C24-1..4; this issue owns the one-command, one-run contract and the bundle layout"* — is correct and #727 restated it verbatim. Absorbing #727 does not pull any artifact-kind scope in.
- **The pass-2 feature-boundary comment above stands unchanged.** #536, #537, #538, #539 and this issue remain five distinct issues; nothing in that adjudication is disturbed.
- **The cross-cluster SVG-seam flag stands.** #536 (print figure), #546 (tactile) and #551 (gallery) all emit SVG; the determinism obligation (bundled font, no OS font fallback) should be owned once in #536 and consumed. This issue consumes #536's SVG through the bundle and does not get a vote.
- **The `getGraphics()`-free / print-theme dependency noted on #289** applies here too: a print theme seam must be theme-independent, or a user's active dark theme leaks into handout figures. That contract is #289 §7.1's and #707's; this bundle inherits it.

---

### D. Tier consequence — for the pass that acts on this

**This feature now has no filed task.** #727 was its sole child, so once #727 closes, #541 is a `tier:feature` whose acceptance criteria are, after this comment, stated at implementation granularity. A later pass must pick one of two dispositions and record it:

- **(a)** relabel #541 `tier:task` and attach it to CAP-24 (#505) directly — defensible, because the bundle is one command with one test and does not decompose further; or
- **(b)** keep #541 `tier:feature` and file exactly one replacement task carrying §A and §B above.

Do **not** leave it as a feature with an empty roster. Whichever is chosen, this comment is the complete source for the task-level content.

**Do not close #727 manually** — stage 3 closes after verification.

DISPOSITION (adversarial review, slice ux-docs): the empty roster left by the dedup pass is resolved — #541 stays `tier:feature` and gets a two-task roster.

**The defect.** #727's absorbing comment flagged that closing it left this feature with **no children at all**, recorded two acceptable dispositions — relabel #541 `tier:task`, or file exactly one replacement task — and required one be chosen. Neither was. A `tier:feature` with an empty roster is not a scheduling inconvenience: it is an issue nobody can pick up, because the tier contract says work is picked up at task level.

**Neither offered disposition is correct, and the third one is.**

- *Relabel #541 `tier:task`* would parent a task directly on capstone #505, breaking the capstone → feature → task chain this restructuring exists to establish. It also understates the work: a headless command, an arity contract, an in-tree layout document, a determinism claim over four artifact kinds and a LaTeX CI leg is not one PR.
- *File exactly one replacement task* re-creates the near-verbatim shape the dedup pass closed — the next dedup pass reads "the only task against #541, whose outcome is #541's whole outcome" and closes it again. That is a loop, not a resolution.
- **Split.** Two tasks along a seam that is real, so each fails for its own reason and lands as its own PR.

**The roster, filed:**

| Task | Owns | Fails when |
|---|---|---|
| #874 TASK-C541-1 | the command, the one-circuit/one-run arity contract, the documented bundle layout, byte-identical SVG/PDF/TikZ/WaveJSON | a second run is silently defaulted, or a re-run differs |
| #875 TASK-C541-2 | the in-tree LaTeX handout, `HandoutBundleTest`, and the assertion that no two artifacts in one bundle came from two runs | five files exist but two of them are from different runs |

**The seam is load-bearing, not cosmetic.** #541's AC-1 and AC-2 are separable claims and the dedup comment's migrated content proves it: AC-2's refusal clause ("a second run, or none, is refused by name") is a property of the command, checkable with no LaTeX toolchain present; AC-1's "the in-tree LaTeX document builds clean in CI" is a property of a consumer, checkable with no arity logic exercised. Everything #727 carried forward is preserved: the refusal clause and PDF-in-the-deterministic-set land in #874, AC-5's in-tree bundle layout lands in #874 criterion 4, the resolved `ordering_after` (#711, #714, #718, #722, each its producing feature's *last* task) lands in #874 with its table, and the PF-4 promotion-to-criterion is carried in **both** so the animation can only drop by a `REPLAN:` on #505.

**One criterion strengthened, and why.** #541's AC-1 as written — "produces all five artifact kinds, and the LaTeX document builds clean" — cannot fail on the defect the feature exists to prevent. Five files from five different runs satisfy it. #874 criterion 5 makes each artifact record its run identity and #875 criterion 2 asserts they agree, with a planted mismatch recorded as the negative check. Without that pair, CAP-24 risk 4 is stated in the Outcome and asserted nowhere.

`band_mw: 1-2` is unchanged and is split 0.5-1 / 0.5-1 across the two tasks.

## Cross-cluster boundary flags (feature deduplication, pass 1)

This issue was cleared against its CAP-29 siblings (#556, #559, #561) and against #323 — all distinct, see the note on #556. Two **cross-cluster** boundary questions were raised during that pass and are recorded here rather than acted on, because the counterpart issues sit outside this deduplication cluster and no comment was posted on them.

**1. "laid-out" vs #62 (schematic auto-layout for imported netlists).** This issue's title promises a *"working, laid-out circuit."* #62 owns the auto-layout engine for imported netlists (heuristic layered layout; ELK only out-of-process), and #323's § 1 records the layout seam — `src/jls/hdl/layout/SchematicLayouter.java`, alongside `HeuristicLayeredLayouter`, `LayoutGraph`, `LayoutMetrics` and `LayoutInvariants` — as shipping engine-neutral, with a coordinate-preserving engine plugged into it as **separate work informed by #62**.

The body of this issue does not claim a layout engine, and `.dig` files carry their own element coordinates, so the most likely reading is that "laid-out" means *source coordinates honoured*, which needs no engine. **That reading should be made explicit before this issue is executed.** If instead this importer intends to *generate* placement for constructs whose source coordinates cannot be honoured, it is re-owning #62's engine, and the correct resolution is a dependency edge on #62 — not a second layouter. Flagged, not resolved; no scope was moved.

**2. Boundary vs the `.dig` test-vector importer (CAP-29 sibling, cluster C).** Same source tool, deliberately split deliverables. This issue's own boundary note already states it: *"Embedded test-case translation is **not** in this feature — FEAT-C29-5 owns turning `.dig` test sections into runnable `-t` vector files. This importer must parse and preserve those sections so FEAT-C29-5 can consume them."*

The split is **confirmed intentional and correct**, and it mirrors a seam already drawn a generation earlier: #323's § 1 cedes *"the test-vector half of a course"* to the autograding feature for exactly the same reason. The obligation this creates is one-directional and easy to lose — **this importer must not discard the test sections it does not consume.** That preservation requirement is the load-bearing half of the boundary; a `.dig` importer that parses circuits correctly but drops the test sections silently leaves its sibling with nothing to read, and would do so while passing all five of this issue's own ACs. Worth an explicit AC if this issue is ever revised.

Neither flag is a duplicate finding. No content migrated; this issue stands as filed.

5227255089.body:
## Adversarial review, core-format slice — the Outcome overstates what is missing, and one ordering edge points at an unfiled component

Two corrections. Neither changes this feature's direction (table → circuit), which is genuinely
absent and correctly the interesting half of CAP-31.

### 1. CORRECTNESS: "a student types or edits a truth table" already ships

The Outcome sentence — *"A student types or edits a truth table and gets back a drawn, laid-out
two-level circuit"* — bundles a shipped capability with an absent one, and AC-4 ("Table-entry bounds
match the analysis bounds") is written as though table entry were being built here.

Verified on master `07a0bea`: `jls.elem.TruthTable` (1,491 lines, a registered element type) plus
`jls.edit.TruthTableEditor` and `jls.edit.DisplayBool` already give a student named inputs and
outputs, cell-by-cell editing, and **don't-cares as a first-class cell value** (`TruthTable.java:79`
— entries are "0, 1 or 2 (don't care)"; `makeDontCare` `:869`, `undoDontCare` `:985`;
`DisplayBool:161` renders `x`). It saves, loads, round-trips and simulates.

**Read the Outcome as:** *a truth table — typed into the shipped table element, or extracted by
#563 — becomes a drawn, laid-out two-level circuit built from the existing palette.* The entry half
is not scope; the **bound** on entry is (there is none today: `grep -n "MAX\|maxInputs" src/jls/elem/TruthTable.java`
returns nothing, and `addInput` doubles the row count with no ceiling). AC-4 is therefore correct in
substance and mis-framed in prose: it is *adding* a bound to a shipped editor, not stating a property
of one being built. The full correction is on #652 (TASK-C565-1), which carried the same error into
its AC-1.

Consequence for planning: `band_mw: "2-4"` was priced with table entry inside it. The residual is the
minimizer→netlist construction, palette instantiation, layout reuse and the round trip. Re-band at
pickup.

### 2. ORDERING: the second boundary bullet depends on a component nobody had filed

> Round-trip verification depends on FEAT-C31-1's extractor path, which in turn consumes CAP-09
> #306's shared combinational-subgraph extractor.

No filed issue delivered that extractor — searched at review time, `combinational subgraph` /
`combinational cone` / `extractor` matched only the CAP-31 family and #306's own capstone body, and
CAP-09 has no feature or task that owns cone identification. It is now filed as **#872
(TASK-C563-0)**, `part_of_feature: 563`, `shared_with: [306]`. Read the bullet as: *…which in turn
consumes #872, the shared combinational-cone extractor.* #641 and #563 have had their `ordering_after`
re-pointed the same way; #306 has been notified.

### 3. One criterion that cannot currently be evaluated, and how to fix it

**AC-3** — *"The generated layout is placed and routed legibly using the #62 heuristic-layouter
lineage **where available**"* — is unfalsifiable as written. "Where available" means the criterion
passes whether or not the layouter exists, and "legibly" has no test. #62 (HDL Stage 2 companion:
schematic auto-layout for imported netlists) is open and unlanded, so today "where available" resolves
to "not available" and AC-3 is vacuously satisfied by any placement at all, including all elements at
the origin.

Make it decidable by splitting the two claims it conflates:

- **AC-3a (must hold unconditionally):** the synthesized result is an ordinary editable circuit —
  every element selectable, movable and deletable, saved through the normal writer, with no locked or
  generated-only marker. This is testable today and is the part that actually matters to a student.
- **AC-3b (conditional, with its condition written down):** *if* #62 has landed at execution time,
  layout goes through it and no second layouter is written; *if not*, a deliberately trivial
  placement ships, a `WAIVED:` comment names #62, and #654 (TASK-C565-3, which declares the #62
  lineage) carries the follow-up. Either way the disposition is recorded rather than left to "where
  available".

The legibility claim itself belongs to #62's rubric, not here — restating it here creates a second,
untested definition of legible.

**AC-3 here is about a check *executing* for a stranger.** A first-time contributor pushes to their own fork and gets a green/red verdict with no maintainer approval step. ## Boundary record (feature deduplication, pass 2) — this issue was examined against #212, #223 and #330, and NOT merged

This issue was considered for a merge with **#212** (ServiceLoader element-provider API) and for a three-way with **#330** (FEAT-050, since closed as a duplicate of #212). **No merge is recorded.** The adjudication was written onto #212 and #223 in pass 1; it is mirrored here so this side carries it too, and so a later pass does not re-open the question.

**Your own Notes block is what settled it**, and it held up under scrutiny:

> this issue owns only the publication and stability-guarantee layer. The catalog mechanics stay in #223; the single in-tree loading class stays in #399; the ServiceLoader element-provider mechanism stays in #212. This feature consumes all three.

### The separating tests, recorded so the boundary is checkable rather than asserted

- **Against #212.** #212's I1–I4 are *mechanism* predictions: a fixture provider jar on the classpath round-trips a `.jls` file, the discovered type is placeable from the generated palette, boot-time seam contributions equal built-ins ∪ discovered, and a shipped doc states the #222 trusted-extension stance. **Every one of those passes with no published API surface at all** — an in-tree fixture jar and an in-tree trust note satisfy them. **AC-2 and AC-4 are inexpressible in #212's terms**: #212 has no per-seam stability taxonomy and no deprecation policy (its `apiVersion` row says only "major = break, no ranges"), and its I1 is deliberately satisfied by a fixture *the maintainer builds*.
- **Against #223.** #223's criteria 1–4 are all satisfiable with the catalog living only in `docs/` inside the repository, read by contributors who have a checkout. **AC-4 is unsatisfiable in that world.** #223's only stability rule is narrower and different in kind — point ids are stable once shipped and never renamed, because manifests and diagnostics name them. That is *id* stability, an internal correctness constraint; it says nothing about whether a seam's *contract type* may change or what notice a breaking change gets, which is this issue's subject.

**The near-collision worth naming.** #212's third planned task ("Trust & API docs") is adjacent to AC-1/AC-2 but answers a different question. **#212's document answers "is this code sandboxed?"** (no, by explicit opt-in — the #222 stance at `ARCHITECTURE.md#L295`). **This issue's document answers "will this API still be here next release?"** A provider author needs both; merging them would make the security statement hostage to a publication schedule.

### Four consequences carried forward

1. **AC-4 strictly subsumes #212's I1** — an outside author following published instructions, rather than the maintainer running a fixture. When this issue is scheduled, **#212's I1 should be recorded as subsumed rather than run twice.**
2. **A row still `pending` in #223's catalog is not a supported extension point** and must not appear in AC-1's published set as though it were. Recommended handling: **publish only the typed-now rows and mark the rest as unpublished rather than as "evolving."** Counted at `2d0ca9d`: four rows `typed now`, three `pending` (`hdl.importer` #61/#62, `app.command` #84, `gui.theme` #76). The catalog stays the single source; the publication is a projection of it.
3. **The freeze in `ordering_after` is load-bearing in both directions.** If a seam is published as *frozen*, #223's `blocked_by` owners (#61/#62, #84, #76) can no longer land a contract that changes that row's type or cardinality without a deprecation cycle. Publish after those contracts land, or publish the row as *evolving*.
4. **`ordering_after: #399` assumes #399 is a single in-tree loading class**, which matches #399's `ForeignElement` design. If #399's shape changes, AC-3's walkthrough is stale — a `REPLAN:` that must reach both issues.

### One upstream bookkeeping change that touches this issue's ordering

**#330 (FEAT-050) closed in this pass as a duplicate of #212**, with **#223 as co-survivor** for the registry-dispatch and catalog half. #399 was filed as #330's TASK-0107 child and its `part_of_feature: 330` field is now stale — **it re-homes to `part_of_feature: 212`**. `ordering_after`'s two entries (#223, #399) are both unaffected in substance: #223 survives unchanged, and #399 remains the external-element-jar task this issue's AC-3 walks through. No edit to this issue is required; the note exists so the #330 reference is not encountered later as a dangling one.

No merge is recorded. This issue remains open with distinct scope.

Pass 1 adjudicated this issue against #76 and #75 and recorded the findings on those two; this comment puts them here, on the issue an implementer of FEAT-C30-5 will read. Three constraints, all load-bearing.

**1. Dark mode is not owned twice — the chain is single, and this issue is already correct.** AC-1 disclaims the scope outright (*"Dark mode lands via #289; this issue adds no dark-mode scope of its own"*). Ownership runs **#76 → #289**; this feature consumes (rule 3(b)). Keep AC-1 exactly as written; the moment it acquires dark-mode implementation detail, #289 and this issue become a real duplicate. Related-but-distinct neighbours: #286 (themed chrome), #381 (#76/#73 residual carrying the DARK variant and the scaling matrix).

**2. Keybinding persistence belongs on #76's existing preference surface, not a new store.** AC-3 wants a persisted, user-editable rebinding surface with reset-to-defaults. #75 §3 records *"Durable state: none — no persisted keymap; bindings are code + policy"*, so this is genuinely new scope with no owner — but the storage seam already exists: `UserPrefs` on `java.util.prefs` with the in-memory sandbox fallback (`UserPrefs.java#L31-L38`, round-trips pinned by `UserPrefsTest`), and #76 carries a **planned settings dialog** task explicitly scoped as *"consolidating theme, colors, undo depth, recent files, last directory"*. The keybinding map is a key on that surface and the rebinding UI is a page in that dialog. Do not stand up a second preferences store or a second settings window; coordinate through #76's REPLAN protocol. #76's §4 invariant 5 (all user prompts through the headless-aware `TellUser`, never raw `JOptionPane` — the #81 ratchet) binds any dialog added here.

**3. A rebinding UI that bypasses `MenuAcceleratorPolicy` silently breaks #75.** #75 owns binding **policy** and platform-correct defaults (`MenuAcceleratorPolicy`, `KeyboardConstructionPolicy`), and its invariant 3 is guarded by `HotkeysHelpAccuracyTest`, which pins `hotkeys.html` against `EditOp` drift. A user-editable keymap that writes accelerators directly onto menu items rather than through the policy layer will not be caught by that test until the help page has already gone stale. Boundary: **#75 owns binding policy and defaults; this feature owns user-editable persisted rebinding over it** — and the rebinding path must render through the same policy, with `hotkeys.html` generation made keymap-aware rather than left asserting defaults.

**4. Fences with CAP-37.** #596 is CAP-37's designated forever-bucket and explicitly disclaims this issue's headline items — dark mode and rebindable keys are not "small stuff" to be picked up there. Conversely, #594 owns keyboard **palette** navigation and #593 owns canvas manipulation gestures; neither is this feature's keybinding surface. 5227450446.body:
## ORDERING CORRECTION (round-2 review, slice: ordering-coherence) — a ≈0 mw outreach action is ordered behind a 12–20 mw editor refactor; the edge is split by criterion

This comment supersedes the `ordering_after` line of the machine block. No acceptance criterion is struck, reworded or moved, and no scope changes.

### 1. The defect

```yaml
ordering_after: ["FEAT-C30-1 #567", "FEAT-C30-2 #568", "#316 (FEAT-008 — the PF-3 prerequisite, owned by CAP-00)"]
```

Read literally — and machine blocks are read literally — this feature may not begin until the issue-template work, the good-first-issue funnel, **and the SimpleEditor decomposition** have all landed. #316 is FEAT-008's residual; #508 prices FEAT-008's decomposition at 12–20 mw and explicitly holds it *"to its own 3.5-wk checkpoint."*

Behind that gate sits **AC-1**: post a comment on the two 2026 PRs this repo bounced (#4/#5, #187) saying their fixes were merged by other means, and inviting the authors back.

That action is the review's stated **highest-leverage move in the whole programme** — #508 §3 item 1, *"Reconcile with the live user base (≈0 mw, highest leverage)"*, and half of queue row 0. It costs one comment each. It is currently graph-blocked behind the largest editor refactor in the tracker, which is itself a checkpoint-gated item the review declined to fund up front. Nothing in AC-1 touches the editor, the templates or the funnel.

### 2. Why only one criterion carries the gate

The gate is real — for AC-2, and AC-2 says so itself:

> AC-2: A named-invitation list of Digital's rejected-PR authors exists, and **invitations go out only after #567, #568, and #316 have landed** (per the capstone's PF-1..3 gate).

That is the correct shape of the constraint and the reason for it is sound: inviting strangers to contribute before there is a template to file against, a shelf to pick from, and a codebase whose largest class has been decomposed is inviting them to bounce a second time. The defect is that the criterion-scoped gate was lifted verbatim into a feature-scoped `ordering_after`, which is a strictly stronger statement than the criterion it came from.

| Criterion | Needs #567 / #568 / #316? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| AC-1 — comment on #4/#5 and #187, state the merged-by-other-means outcome, invite back | **No** | Two comments to people who already engaged this repo on their own initiative. They are not being recruited into a cold on-ramp; they are being answered. |
| AC-2 — named-invitation list for Digital's rejected-PR authors, invitations sent | **Yes** — unchanged | The criterion's own text states the gate. Cold outreach needs the on-ramp to exist. |
| AC-3 — CONTRIBUTING publishes the <48h first-response / <1wk first-merge-decision objectives | **No** | A published service objective is a commitment the maintainer makes, not a feature of the codebase. Publishing it *before* the funnel is what makes AC-4's record start accruing. |
| AC-4 — rolling record shows actual first-response times | **No** (starts with AC-3) | It measures elapsed time on whatever arrives. Starting it late does not improve it; it just shortens the window the capstone's median-<48h-over-a-quarter bar can be computed over. |
| AC-5 — kill-criterion hook (two quarters post-PF-1..4 with zero external PRs) | **Yes**, by construction | Its clock is defined relative to PF-1..4 landing. |

### 3. The correction

```yaml
ordering_after: []                                  # was: [567, 568, 316]
ordering_after_by_criterion:
  AC-1: []                                          # ready now — #508 queue item 0
  AC-2: [567, 568, 316]                             # unchanged; the criterion's own gate
  AC-3: []                                          # ready now
  AC-4: [571-AC-3]                                  # starts when AC-3 publishes
  AC-5: [567, 568, 316]                             # clock is defined off PF-1..4
```

AC-4's bar is *measurable from* the record, so an early start strictly helps: the quarter the capstone grades has to come from somewhere.

### 4. One consequence worth stating out loud

AC-3 publishes a **<48h first-response objective**. Publishing it is free; *keeping* it is a standing obligation on a bus-factor-1 project, and this feature's own band already says `"0.5-1 + ongoing"`. Unblocking AC-3 is not a recommendation to publish it this week — it is a statement that nothing on the graph prevents it, and that the decision is a maintainer commitment call rather than a dependency. AC-5 exists precisely so the commitment has an exit; the exit is not weakened by starting the clock earlier.

### 5. Mirror

Posted on **#316** in the same pass, recording that the #571 edge is narrowed to AC-2/AC-5 and that #316 remains a genuine prerequisite for those two.

## Boundary note: #577 / #578 (feature deduplication, pass 1)

This pair entered pass 1 as **the strongest merge candidate in its cluster** — #577's "the first course kit" and #578's "one complete worked course" read as the same artifact named twice. Close reading refutes that. **Verdict: no merge.** Recording the refutation in detail, because the surface reading is genuinely persuasive and a later pass will otherwise re-derive it.

**They are not the same artifact.** #578's Outcome names its worked instance explicitly, and it is not this one: *"The Donzellini-mapped pack from **FEAT-C33-1** ships as the complete worked instance, so the convention is demonstrated rather than merely asserted."* FEAT-C33-1 is **#575** — 8+ original labs authored against the standard text. #575 carries the matching statement from its side ("Shipped as the complete worked instance of the kit convention in FEAT-C33-4"). So #578's AC-3 is discharged by #575's pack, not by this issue's corpus.

**What "first course kit" means here is different in kind.** This issue's artifact is the **WashU CSE 260M corpus** — a real course's labs, from a named instructor, arriving with a provenance and licensing story that no other kit in the set has:

- AC-1 commits the corpus as **compatibility fixtures** with recorded provenance, under a CI lane that loads + simulates + grades every fixture on every change. That is a regression-detection outcome that exists whether or not a kit ever ships.
- AC-2 requires any circuit that fails to load or grades differently than on the origin fork to be a **named, dispositioned finding** — never silently dropped. This is a migration-fidelity obligation against an external baseline; nothing in #578 has an origin fork to differ from.
- AC-3 gates the kit half on **written content licensing with Dr. Siever**, and states the fallback plainly: absent agreement, the fixtures land as compatibility fixtures only and the kit half is held. #578 has no such external gate.

**The dependency runs one way.** This issue's AC-4 says the adapted kit "conforms to the packaging convention of FEAT-C33-4 and runs through the assignment workflow of FEAT-C33-2" — it **consumes** #578's convention and #576's workflow. #578 in turn owns the layout spec, the validator, the content-license policy and the third-party authoring doc, none of which appears here. Rule 3(b)/3(c), not 3-duplicate.

**The real tension, stated so it is not mistaken for duplication later:** the set now contains two plausible referents for "the flagship kit" — #575's Donzellini pack (the convention's designated worked instance) and this issue's CSE 260M corpus (the capstone's demo slice, because it is *"the only course kit backed by a real course, a named instructor and a stated conditional interest rather than a hypothesis"*). Both readings are defensible and the two issues currently answer the question differently. That is a **naming/positioning question for the capstone**, not a duplicate outcome, and merging would destroy either the validator's independent subject or the corpus's fixture-and-provenance work.

**Also recorded:** this issue's tie to #509 is a reference, not an absorption — #509 keeps the adoption relationship, the fork-delta audit, release-channel policy and the migration; this issue owns only the in-tree artifacts, and satisfies #509's AC-3 via its own AC-1. ## Boundary note (feature deduplication, pass 1)

Cluster G pass 1 checked this issue against **#524** (cross-cluster, FEAT-C21-1 — "the headless CLI stops being observed behavior and becomes a frozen, versioned promise") and against **#585 AC-4**. **No merge** in either case. #524 is in cluster C and nothing was posted there; the flag is recorded here.

### #587 vs #524 — same surface, different gates (rule 3(c))

The suspicion was that *"an undocumented flag fails the build"* and *"the CLI is a frozen versioned promise"* are one gate specified twice. They are not:

- **#524 freezes behaviour and makes breaking it a versioned event.** Its artifact is a contract document specifying invocation forms, every exit status including status 3, artifact output paths and the xUnit report schema, each clause exercised by `CliContractConformanceTest`; plus a semver-and-deprecation-window ratchet, a seeded-violation falsification transcript, and a contract version queryable from the CLI so an adapter can refuse an incompatible build by name. - **#587 makes documentation unable to lie.** Its AC-1 is the doc side of a triangle #524 does not touch: every flag named in `docs/batch-interface.md`, README and the help pages resolves to a `FLAGS` entry, and every `FLAGS` entry is documented somewhere the assertion names. This issue's own boundary note already establishes that `CliFlagTableTest` (#71) binds `FLAGS` to `usage()` and to what the parser accepts but **reads no documentation file at all** — that gap is this issue's ground, and #524 does not close it either.

A flag can be perfectly frozen and versioned while being undocumented (#524 green, #587 red), and perfectly documented while drifting between releases with no deprecation window (#587 green, #524 red).

**Recommended, not decided:** both read the `FLAGS` table, and they should read it through one accessor rather than two hand-rolled reflections, so the frozen contract and the documented set cannot disagree about what a flag *is*. If #524 lands first, its contract document becomes one more file this issue's AC-1 must assert against — it is documentation like any other, and a contract clause naming a flag the parser rejects should turn this ratchet red.

### #587 vs #585 AC-4 — link integrity is not claim accuracy

#585 AC-4 checks the hosted site for dead cross-links with the same strictness the in-jar tree gets. This issue checks whether resolving pages tell the truth about ports, parameters, accelerators and flags. A page can resolve perfectly and be entirely wrong. Distinct; no overlap in acceptance criteria.

5227298980.body:
## AC-3 contradicts KC-38-1 and a shipped architectural invariant; AC-1 is not evaluable until #416 lands. Both corrected here.

Adversarial review of the `hdl-physical` slice, verified against `master`. Two defects, one of which would cause wrong work to be built. This comment supersedes AC-1 and AC-3 of the body above.

**First, the good news — the substrate claims all check out.** `Boards.all()` exists (`src/jls/hdl/board/Boards.java:88`); `-board` / `-pins` exist (`src/jls/JLSStart.java:111-114`, dispatched at `:387-427`); `PcfEmitter.emit(model, board, bindings)` exists (`:427`); `scripts/icestick-handoff.sh` exists; `docs/component-naming.md` exists. The "surface over the existing headless path, not a second implementation" framing is sound and AC-5 is well-posed.

### 1. AC-3 asks for something this feature's own kill criterion forbids, and that `src/` has never done

**AC-3 as written:** *"One action from the dialog runs export + constraint emission + **the handoff script** and reports the outcome in the GUI; no step requires a terminal."*

**KC-38-1, three lines below it:** *"no vendor-toolchain process driving in this surface."*

These cannot both hold. Running `scripts/icestick-handoff.sh` from a dialog **is** process driving, and the script's whole job is to drive `yosys`, `nextpnr-ice40`, `icepack` and `openFPGALoader`. The kill criterion is not a hedge against AC-3; it is its negation.

The conflict is not only internal. Measured on `master`:

```
$ grep -rn "ProcessBuilder\|Runtime.getRuntime().exec" src/ | wc -l
0
```

**There is not one subprocess spawn in the entire shipped source tree**, and that is a deliberate, load-bearing invariant, not an accident:

- **#359 §4 invariant 1** states it as a preservation requirement — *"No subprocess in `src/`. External tools are invoked from `test/` only, through `ToolLocator`. The single self-contained offline jar stays offline: a student who never installs a toolchain must still get a working JLS"* — and carries a DoD line requiring `git grep -l "ProcessBuilder" -- src/` to still return nothing at close.
- **`scripts/icestick-handoff.sh` says so in its own header**: *"JLS emits the RTL and the pin constraints; it does NOT synthesize, place, route, pack, or flash anything (issue #215 H2: **delegate, do not reimplement**)."*

So AC-3 as written would have a task author put the first `ProcessBuilder` into `src/`, breaking an invariant another open feature is committed to preserving and turning the offline jar into something that behaves differently depending on whether a student has an FPGA toolchain installed. **This is exactly the wrong work, and #636 (TASK-C597-3) is the issue scheduled to do it.** Corrected there too.

**AC-3 is replaced by:**

> **AC-3 (corrected).** One action from the dialog produces **every artifact the handoff needs** — the exported RTL and the constraint file — into a user-chosen directory, and presents the exact handoff command line to run, copyable, with the tool prerequisites named. The GUI reports what it produced and where. **No process is spawned from `src/`**, and `grep -r "ProcessBuilder" src/` still returns nothing at close.
>
> The honest claim this feature can make is *"no terminal to produce the artifacts"*, not *"no terminal at all."* The bitstream step delegates to tools JLS deliberately does not bundle, and a student without them installed must get a clear statement of what to install rather than an opaque failure from a spawned process.

If the maintainer wants true one-click flashing, that is a **separate, larger decision** — it makes an external toolchain a runtime dependency of the GUI, needs a per-platform tool-location story, needs process output surfaced in a dialog, and needs #359 invariant 1 renegotiated with its owner. It is not a task under a "surface over the existing headless path" feature, and it must not be smuggled in as one bullet.

### 2. AC-1 cannot be evidenced today — the extension it asserts has no seam and no second instance

**AC-1:** *"the board picker's entries are read from `Boards.all()`, so a board added by #264/#416 appears with no GUI change."* #632 AC-1 sharpens it to *"asserted by a test that adds a synthetic board and observes it appear with no GUI source change."*

On `master`:

```java
private static final Board ICESTICK = new Board("icestick", ...);   // Boards.java:34
private static final List<Board> ALL = List.of(ICESTICK);           // Boards.java:81
public static List<Board> all() { return ALL; }                     // Boards.java:88
```

- **`ALL` is a private `List.of` with no registration seam.** A test cannot add a synthetic board without editing `Boards.java` or resorting to reflection — and a reflective test is not a shippable assertion (the same objection #492 raises about its own probe).
- **There is exactly one board, and exactly one `Board.Format` constant** (`Board.java:35-41`, `PCF("pcf")`). So "a second board appears with no GUI change" has no second board to appear.

The negative half is evidenceable today and is the part that actually carries the weight — #632 AC-4 already states it: *a test asserts the GUI holds no board list, no format list and no pin table of its own.* The positive half is not.

**AC-1 is replaced by:**

> **AC-1 (corrected).** The picker is populated by calling `Boards.all()` and `Board`'s accessors, and holds no board list, format list or pin table of its own — asserted by a structural test over the GUI sources (the evidenceable form, and the one that actually prevents the drift). **The "a new board appears with no GUI change" claim is evidenced when #416 lands its second board**, by re-running the picker test unchanged and observing two entries. Until then it is an unverified design intent, stated as such, not an acceptance criterion presented as met.
>
> Alternatively, if a test seam on `Boards` is wanted sooner, **it is scoped and owned by #264** — not invented here. This feature must not add a registration API to `jls.hdl.board` under cover of "putting a GUI on it."

**Ordering consequence:** `ordering_after: [264, 288]` is right for the code, but **#416 is a real prerequisite for AC-1's evidence** and is currently carried only as a boundary note ("consumed, not duplicated"). Either write the edge for the evidence, or restate AC-1 as above and let #416 discharge it later — the second is recommended, since blocking the whole GUI flow on a second board would be over-ordering. Recorded on #416 by reference.

### 3. AC-2 stands, with one sharpening

*"GUI and CLI paths emit byte-identical constraint files for the same design and bindings"* is well-posed, evaluable today, and is the strongest criterion in the set — `PcfEmitter.emit` and `PinBindings.parse` are both reachable from both paths. Sharpening: the test must drive the **CLI path end to end** (through the `-board`/`-pins` argument handling at `JLSStart.java:387-427`), not merely call `PcfEmitter.emit` twice with the same arguments. Calling the same function twice proves the function is deterministic, not that the two paths agree.

Also inherit the error-aggregation idiom the substrate already establishes: `PinBindings.parse` collects **every** malformed line and reports them together, *"so the user learns the full repair job from a single failure."* A dialog that rejects the first bad binding and stops is a regression against the CLI it is wrapping — which matters for #638 (unassigned port / wrong-direction binding messages).

### 4. KC-38-2 is well-formed and should be kept

*"if #264's stage 2 lands the GUI flow itself, this feature is consumed rather than rebuilt"* — this is a good kill criterion and one of the few in the slice with a concrete trigger. Keep it, and note that #264 is the right place to check before starting any child here.

## Boundary: #612 vs #621 vs #629 — three untrusted-parse tasks, one per format, NOT duplicates

Stage 2 (MIGRATE) of the feature-to-task pass checked the newly filed C29 importer-suite tasks against each other. Three of them are the "parse the foreign file as hostile input" slice of three different importers, all carrying `ordering_after: [314]` and all citing the same #38 / CAP-16 hardening standard. Diffed by prose they read as one task filed three times. Recording the split here, on the lowest number.

| Issue | Parent | Substrate | Attack surface it is actually defending |
|---|---|---|---|
| **#612** (this issue) | **#558** FEAT-C29-2 (`.dig`) | XStream **XML** | XXE, billion-laughs, external DTD, SSRF-via-entity — one test per vector; external entities, doctype declarations and entity resolution all disabled. Plus the unique obligation to preserve Digital's **embedded test sections byte-recoverably** for #635/#637/#639 |
| **#621** | **#559** FEAT-C29-3 (`.cv`) | plain **JSON** | deep nesting, oversized document, duplicate keys, unexpected types — a named limit in every diagnostic. No entity model exists, so no XXE analogue. Plus preserving per-circuit structure and inter-circuit references for #624's hierarchy rebuild |
| **#629** | **#561** FEAT-C29-4 (Falstad) | line-oriented **text**, neither XML nor JSON | unbounded line length, unbounded line count, out-of-range numeric fields, unknown element codes; **numeric overflow into a valid-looking value** is the hazard with no analogue in the other two, because there is no schema to lean on |

**Not duplicates.** Three parse substrates, three disjoint threat sets, three different downstream obligations on what the parse must *preserve*. Merging any pair would fuse an entity-expansion review with a numeric-bounds review. This is a shared *discipline* (rule 3(b) — siblings inheriting one prerequisite standard), not a shared outcome. #556's own boundary note on #556 records the same finding at the feature level for #558/#559/#561.

**Three coordination points an executor of any of them needs.**

1. **#451 (TASK-0054) is the tree's first XML parse and sets the precedent.** #451 §7.5 is explicit that its hardened parser factory configuration *must not become a shared utility in that task* — "it is the tree's first and its shape should be reviewed once, in context, before a second caller fixes it." #612 is that second caller. Whoever lands second should promote the configuration deliberately rather than copy it; #621 and #629 inherit the *discipline* (one test per vector, no path from document content to filesystem or network, no partial model returned) but share no parser code with it.
2. **"No partial model on failure" is stated identically in all three** (#612 AC-3, #621 AC-3, #629 AC-3) and is the same invariant #323 §4.1 and `NetlistImporter.java:41-47` already carry. It is one rule, three enforcement points — do not let one of the three weaken it to "refuse after building".
3. **The `location` field is the real shared contract.** #608 (TASK-C556-1) AC-4 names the Falstad text format as the *worked example* proving `location` can name a position in a non-XML source, and #629 AC-4 is the matching obligation from the parse side. So #629 and #608 are load-bearing on each other: if #629's per-element source location is coarser than a line, #608's AC-4 cannot be demonstrated. Neither owns the other; both must land with the same notion of a location.

**Disposition.** #612, #621 and #629 all stay open in their existing tiers under their existing parents (#558, #559, #561). Nothing superseded, nothing closed.

There is **no subprocess spawn anywhere in the shipped source tree**, and that is deliberate:

- **#597's own KC-38-1** says *"no vendor-toolchain process driving in this surface"* — which AC-3 directly contradicts. The feature contradicts itself, and this task is the one that would resolve the contradiction by writing code.
- **#359 §4 invariant 1**: *"No subprocess in `src/`. External tools are invoked from `test/` only, through `ToolLocator`. The single self-contained offline jar stays offline: a student who never installs a toolchain must still get a working JLS."* #359 carries a DoD line requiring that grep to still return nothing at close.
- **`scripts/icestick-handoff.sh`'s own header**: *"JLS emits the RTL and the pin constraints; it does NOT synthesize, place, route, pack, or flash anything (issue #215 H2: **delegate, do not reimplement**)."*

Implementing "one button carries the design to a programmed board" as written means spawning `yosys`, `nextpnr-ice40`, `icepack` and `openFPGALoader` from the GUI. That makes an external FPGA toolchain a de-facto runtime dependency of the editor, gives the offline jar behaviour that varies with what the user has installed, and reverses a decision recorded in three places.

### Corrected scope for this task

> **One action from the board dialog produces every artifact the handoff needs** — the exported RTL and the emitted constraint file — into a user-chosen directory, reports exactly what was written and where, and **presents the handoff command line to run, copyable**, with its tool prerequisites named. No process is spawned from `src/`.

Acceptance:

1. One action writes both artifacts; the GUI names each path. Failure at either step reports which step failed and leaves no partial output — matching the CLI's existing all-or-nothing export behaviour.
2. The emitted artifacts are **byte-identical** to what the CLI path produces for the same design and bindings (this is #597 AC-2's guarantee, and this task is where it is exercised end to end).
3. The presented command line is the real one — derived from the board definition and the chosen output paths, not a hardcoded string — and it is selectable/copyable from the dialog.
4. `grep -r "ProcessBuilder\|Runtime.getRuntime().exec" src/` returns nothing at the fix commit. **This is a required check, not a nicety.**
5. Keyboard-reachable, stable component names per `docs/component-naming.md`, per #597 AC-4.

### The honest claim, and why it still delivers the outcome

#597's outcome is *"a student takes a drawn circuit to an FPGA board without ever opening a terminal."* The truthful version after this correction is **"no terminal to produce the artifacts"** — the bitstream step delegates to tools JLS deliberately does not bundle. That is a real and worthwhile improvement over today (where the student must know the CLI flags, the board name and the bindings file format), and it is achievable without breaking anything.

A student without the toolchain installed gets a clear statement of what to install, which is strictly better than an opaque failure from a spawned process they cannot see the output of.

### If true one-click flashing is actually wanted

It is a **separate and much larger decision**, not a bullet under a "surface over the existing headless path" feature. It requires: making an external toolchain a runtime dependency of the GUI; a per-platform tool-location story (`ToolLocator` lives in `test/` and is test-scope); streaming process output into a dialog; a cancellation story for a multi-minute place-and-route; and renegotiating #359 invariant 1 with its owner. File it as its own issue against #522 (CAP-38) with those costs stated, and let the maintainer price it. Do not absorb it here.

**Also note:** #359's evidence records that no real bitstream has ever been produced by this path — *"Only the hermetic stub-PATH selftest runs in CI — fake tools, control-flow assertions only."* Putting a GUI button on a path that has never once produced a bitstream would ship a button whose success case is unverified. The recorded hardware walk that would fix that is #264's / #416's, and it should precede any claim that the flow reaches "a programmed board."

## Adversarial review, core-format slice — ORDERING CORRECTION: `ordering_after: [306]` pointed at nothing

This supersedes the `ordering_after` line of the machine block and the first bullet of **Boundary
notes**.

### Two defects in one edge

**1. The prerequisite was never filed.** The boundary note says the combinational-subgraph extractor
"is #306's component. This task consumes it and must not reimplement it". Searched the tracker at
review time: `combinational subgraph`, `combinational-subgraph`, `combinational cone` and `extractor`
match only the CAP-31 family (#515, #563, #565, #641, #642, #655), #306's own capstone body, and
unrelated HDL/breadboard uses. **CAP-09 has no feature or task that owns cone identification.** An
executor picking this task up is instructed not to build the thing it consumes and has nothing to
consume — so they stall, or they build it here anyway, which is the double-build the note exists to
prevent.

Filed as **#872 (TASK-C563-0)**: one callable pass returning a cone (element set, ordered input
frontier, ordered output frontier, per-signal widths) or a named refusal naming the offending
element; `part_of_feature: 563`, `shared_with: [306]`.

**2. Ordering behind a whole capstone is too coarse even when the capstone is right.** `ordering_after:
[306]` reads as "this task waits for CAP-09", and CAP-09 is a proof-and-counterexample capstone whose
scope — replayable counterexamples, honest UNKNOWN, equivalence checking (#483) — this task needs
none of. Enumerating a 4-input truth table does not wait on a verification capstone. The edge must
name the deliverable, not the capstone that mentions it.

**Read the machine block as:**

```yaml
ordering_after: ["#872 TASK-C563-0 (the combinational-cone extractor)"]
```

and nothing else. #306 is `related`, not blocking.

### Scope consequence: AC-3 and AC-4 need a re-read

- **AC-3 (multi-output cones produce one column per output in one table)** — the *frontier* half of
  that is #872's AC-1: the extractor returns an ordered output frontier, and this task's job is one
  column per entry of it. Do not re-derive the frontier here.
- **AC-4 (multi-bit inputs and outputs are handled with a stated convention — bit expansion vs.
  refusal — and whichever is chosen is tested)** is the one acceptance criterion here that is
  **unfalsifiable as written**: it accepts either answer and so cannot fail. It also silently
  interacts with the bound, because bit expansion multiplies the input count that #642's 2^N refusal
  is measured against — an 8-bit and a 4-bit input is 12 rows-worth of exponent, not 2. Resolve it as
  a decision, here, before the enumerator is written:

  > **Decision (recorded, correctable by a later comment):** multi-bit frontier signals **expand to
  > one table column per bit**, most-significant bit first, matching the existing
  > `TruthTable.makeRowCode` convention (`src/jls/elem/TruthTable.java:1064-1078`, which builds a row
  > code as `val += 1 << pos` over input columns) so an extracted table and a typed table share one
  > column semantics. The input count the bound in #642 is applied to is therefore the **expanded bit
  > count**, not the signal count, and #642's arithmetic message must say so. Refusal on multi-bit
  > input is rejected as the convention: it would make the feature useless on any circuit with a bus,
  > which is most circuits worth analysing.

  AC-4 should be evaluated against that sentence, not against "whichever is chosen".

### Verified on master `07a0bea`, not `2d0ca9d`

Nothing extracts a truth table from drawn logic today, and there is no analyze path: the shipped
`jls.elem.TruthTable` is a *specification* element the user types into
(`jls.edit.TruthTableEditor` + `jls.edit.DisplayBool`), simulated by `TruthTable.react`. This task's
direction — circuit → table — is genuinely absent. The golden oracle AC-1 names ("exhaustive
simulation of the original circuit") is available: `jls.sim.BatchSimulator` runs headless.

## Boundary: #644 vs #650 vs #652 — one truth-table surface, three owners

Stage 2 (MIGRATE) of the feature-to-task pass checked the newly filed C31 analysis tasks against each other. Three of them land in the same editor surface, from three different parent features. Recording the split here, on the lowest number, so none of them silently becomes the owner of the whole panel.

| Issue | Parent | Owns on this surface |
|---|---|---|
| **#644** (this issue) | **#563** FEAT-C31-1 | a student selects a region and **reads its truth table in a view, without leaving the editor** — the read-only extraction display |
| **#650** | **#564** FEAT-C31-2 | **minimized expressions displayed beside their truth table**, and exported as plain text |
| **#652** | **#565** FEAT-C31-3 | a student **types and edits a truth table directly**, within the same bound the analysis path enforces |

**Not duplicates.** Extraction-display, minimization-display and direct-authoring are three distinct capabilities with three distinct failure modes, each pinned by a different parent feature's criteria. They share a rendering surface, not an outcome.

**The coordination point.** All three read or write the same table representation, and #652 explicitly binds itself to "the same bound the analysis path enforces" — that bound is **#642**'s (TASK-C563-2: above the stated input count, show the 2^N arithmetic and refuse). Whichever of the three lands first establishes the table model and the panel; the other two extend it rather than forking a second one. A second truth-table widget in the tree would be the defect this note exists to prevent.

**The loop that closes across the three features.** #655 (TASK-C565-4) asserts that a synthesized circuit's extracted table is identical to the table it was synthesized from — which consumes **#641**'s extraction (TASK-C563-1) and **#653**'s synthesis. That round-trip is the reason the three surfaces must agree on one representation.

**Disposition.** #644, #650 and #652 all stay open in their existing tiers under their existing parents. Nothing superseded, nothing closed.

## Boundary: #646 vs #651 vs #656 — three headless surfaces on one batch CLI

Stage 2 (MIGRATE) of the feature-to-task pass checked the newly filed C31 analysis tasks against each other. Three of them add a headless entry point to the same batch interface, from three different parent features. Recording the split here, on the lowest number.

| Issue | Parent | Headless surface it adds |
|---|---|---|
| **#646** (this issue) | **#563** FEAT-C31-1 | **truth-table extraction** behind a batch flag, with machine-readable output |
| **#651** | **#564** FEAT-C31-2 | **minimization** headless, plus the minimized expression proved equivalent to the original circuit by exhaustive differential test |
| **#656** | **#565** FEAT-C31-3 | **synthesis** headless — a table file in, a circuit file out |

**Not duplicates.** Three different computations, three different output artifacts, three different correctness arguments. They share a CLI, not an outcome.

**The coordination points.**

1. **One flag table, one arity/exclusion policy.** All three add flags to `JLSStart`'s `FLAGS` table. #372 (TASK-0001) is adding a mutual-exclusion declaration to `FlagSpec` and a parse-time rejection naming both offending flags; each of these three must declare its own incompatible pairs there rather than inventing a second refusal path. `CliFlagTableTest` is the existing pin.
2. **The frozen CLI contract.** #686 (TASK-C524-1) freezes the headless CLI contract — invocation, every exit status, artifact paths and the xUnit schema — held by a conformance test, with #687 making a breaking change a versioned event. Three new flags landing after that freeze are contract additions and owe it a conformance case each. Landing before it means the freeze must enumerate them.
3. **Machine-readable output determinism.** Grading and figure paths in this tree require byte-identical artifacts across platforms and runs. Whichever of the three lands first sets the output encoding; the other two match it rather than each choosing their own.

**Disposition.** #646, #651 and #656 all stay open in their existing tiers under their existing parents. Nothing superseded, nothing closed.

## Adversarial review, core-format slice — CORRECTNESS: AC-1 asserts an outcome that is already true on master

This supersedes **AC-1** and the Outcome paragraph's first sentence. AC-2, AC-3 and AC-4 stand, with
AC-4 narrowed below.

### The defect

AC-1 reads:

> A table can be created from scratch with named inputs and outputs and edited cell by cell,
> including don't-care values.

**That ships today.** Verified on master `07a0bea` (not the `2d0ca9d` branch commit #493 records as
unreliable):

- `src/jls/elem/TruthTable.java` — 1,491 lines, a registered element type
  (`jls.elem.ElementRegistry`, `jls.elem.SaveTags`), with the entire editing model already public:
  `addInput(String)` `:610`, `addOutput(String)` `:701`, `removeInput` `:764`, `removeOutput` `:817`,
  `toggleOutput(int,int)` `:854`, **`makeDontCare(int,int)` `:869`**, **`undoDontCare(int,int)`
  `:985`**, `renameInput` `:1081`, `renameOutput` `:1098`, `moveInputLeft/Right` `:1218/:1250`,
  `moveOutputLeft/Right` `:1158/:1188`, `getTable()` `:574`.
- Don't-care is a first-class cell value, not a workaround: `:79` — *"Table entries, indexed by row
  then column (inputs first, then outputs); 0, 1 or 2 (don't care)"* — and `jls.edit.DisplayBool:161`
  renders it as `x`.
- The GUI exists: `jls.edit.TruthTableEditor` (create/edit dialog, input/output name fields) over
  `jls.edit.DisplayBool` (the cell grid, with a per-signal delete/rename/move popup).
- It persists and simulates: `TruthTable.save` `:194`, `setValue` `:290`, `initSim` `:1363`,
  `react` `:1400`, and it is covered by `jls.AllElementsRoundTripTest`.

An acceptance criterion that is green before a line is written is not a criterion. Worse, the title
of this task — *"a student types and edits a truth table directly"* — describes the shipped feature,
so an executor reading title-then-AC-1 will build a second truth-table editor beside the one JLS
already has. That is the wrong-work outcome this correction exists to stop.

### The corrected scope

What is genuinely absent on master is **not** table entry. It is three narrower things:

- **AC-1′ (replaces AC-1): the editing surface gains the bound it has never had.** There is no
  input-count limit anywhere in `TruthTable`: `grep -n "MAX\|maxInputs\|too many" src/jls/elem/TruthTable.java`
  returns nothing, and the only declared constraints are
  `SIGNALS_CONSTRAINT` (`:48` — at least one input and one output) and `entryConstraint(row,col)`
  (`:64` — an entry outside the declared table size, a loader-side rule from #52). `addInput` doubles
  the row count with no ceiling. Evidence for done: adding the (N+1)-th input refuses with the row
  arithmetic, at the same N that #563 and #564 enforce, and **never begins allocating rows** — which
  on today's code means the refusal happens before `addInput` touches the entry array, not after.
- **AC-3 (unchanged, and now the real work): an extracted table (#563) opens in *this* element**, not
  in a second representation. The load-bearing question is whether #563's extractor output is
  materialised as a `jls.elem.TruthTable` (so it is editable, savable and simulable for free) or as a
  separate analysis value that is converted on demand. **Decide it here, before #563 is executed**,
  because #563's table type is chosen there and #655's round-trip assertion compares the two. The
  recommended default is: #563 produces a plain value (a table plus its frontier), and this task
  supplies one conversion into `jls.elem.TruthTable` — because forcing the analysis path to allocate
  a live drawable element in headless batch (#646) is the wrong coupling.
- **AC-4 (narrowed): keyboard operability of the entry surface is genuinely absent, and that is the
  residual worth funding.** `jls.edit.DisplayBool` is a `JPanel implements MouseListener` — cells are
  toggled by click and signals are managed through a click-triggered `JPopupMenu`. There is no key
  binding, no focus traversal within the grid, and no accessible name per cell. AC-4 should be
  evaluated against *that* starting point, and it is the reason this task is not zero-cost after AC-1
  is corrected.

### Two knock-on notes

1. **`band_mw: "1"` was priced for building an editor.** With entry already shipped, the remaining
   work is a bound, one conversion, and a keyboard/a11y pass on an existing `JPanel`. Re-band at
   pickup; do not spend a week re-implementing `DisplayBool`.
2. **`ordering_after: ["TASK-C563-3 (the read-only table view this makes editable)"]` is now wrong in
   its parenthetical.** #644's view is not what this makes editable — an editable surface already
   exists. The real edge is to #563's *table value*, because AC-3 cannot be built or tested before
   there is an extracted table to open. Read it as `ordering_after: [641]`.

## REVISION (adversarial review, grading-ci slice): drop #369 from `ordering_after`, and one criterion needs a falsifiable form

### 1. DEFECT (ordering): `ordering_after: [369, 466]` → `ordering_after: [466]`

Same defect as the parent #524, mirrored here. #369 (FEAT-053) carries `blocked_by: [316, 321, 347]` — the SimpleEditor decomposition (#316), the **Yosys JSON netlist writer** (#321), and the retirement-indexed parity harness (#347). Treating `#369` as a real ordering edge therefore orders *"write the headless CLI contract down and make it executable"* behind a Swing editor refactor and an HDL exporter. It needs neither.

What this task actually consumes is the **verdict channel**: exit status 3, the xUnit report schema, and the artifact paths. All three are #466's, and #466 has been re-scoped by this review to exactly that headless half (its `TestPanel` moved to #214, its cohort-grading command to #757). **#466's `blocked_by` is now empty**, so `ordering_after: [466]` terminates cleanly.

The three issues #369 waits on gate its *other* half — property checking, equivalence and coverage (the unfiled TASK-0112), which is CAP-09's payload and which this contract does not freeze.

### 2. Scope note: this task cannot specify status 3 before #466 defines it — and should not try

The Outcome requires the document to specify *"every exit status including status 3"*. Re-verified at `29afb26` (master; the `2d0ca9d` this lineage cites no longer exists in the repository at all):

- `docs/batch-interface.md` defines exactly three statuses — 0 run completed, 1 runtime failure, 2 usage error — and none means "the run completed and the answer was wrong".
- `grep -c "new FlagSpec" src/jls/JLSStart.java` → `14`; none of them is `-check` or `-report`.
- `src/jls/sim/` contains no `GradeReport` and no xUnit writer.

So both objects this task documents — status 3 and the xUnit schema — are created by #466. **The correct reading of the Boundary is that this task documents and pins #466's semantics; it does not choose them.** In particular #466 fixes that **status 3 is reachable only when `-check` is present, including on error paths** — a malformed expectations file is a usage error (2), never a check failure (3). That rule is a contract clause and belongs in the document with its own conformance-test tag: a grader that scored every submission as failing because of its own configuration error is the failure it prevents.

### 3. AC-4 is the best criterion here and is currently the least testable

AC-4 — *"The document states plainly which observed behaviours are explicitly **not** part of the contract"* — is the clause that decides whether adapter authors build on sand, and it has no falsifier. Two behaviours on master make it concrete, and the document should name both as **excluded**:

- **The `-t` parse-error stream deviation.** `docs/batch-interface.md` records that errors parsing the `-t` file print to *stdout* (not stderr) and exit 1, and advises that grading scripts treat exit status, not stream placement, as the contract. An adapter that parses stdout for those diagnostics is depending on a documented deviation. Name it as out-of-contract rather than freezing it.
- **`displayOutcome`'s four result strings** (`Simulation Complete`, `Simulation Stopped`, `Simulation Time Limit`, `Simulation: No More Activity`), which #466 treats as frozen for compatibility. Decide explicitly whether these are contract or merely stable, because an adapter matching on them will break silently if they are the latter.

**Suggested falsifier for AC-4:** the exclusion list is non-empty, and each entry names a behaviour that a conformance test **asserts is not asserted** — i.e. there is a test that would still pass if that behaviour changed. An exclusion list with no such demonstration is prose.

### 4. AC-3's schema pin has a precondition on #466

AC-3 requires the xUnit schema be *"pinned as a schema artifact, not described in prose alone"*. #466's report deliberately **omits** the `timestamp`, `hostname` and `time` attributes that an xUnit writer adds by default, because those three are what break byte-determinism. Any schema artifact pinned here must therefore permit their absence — a stock xUnit XSD will reject the very reports this contract is freezing. Worth stating in the document, since it is the most likely way an adapter author's off-the-shelf validator disagrees with JLS's own conformance suite.

## Mirror: this task owns the only 300-submission corpus, and it has consumers that never named it

An earlier pass flagged that this task and #697 (TASK-C525-2, `GradescopeCorpusTest`) both speak of a 300-submission corpus, declined to merge them, and left a boundary comment as the recommended next move. Written now, with the ordering edges the flag implied.

### 1. Ruling: exactly one 300-submission corpus exists in the tree, and it is this task's

This task builds the apparatus — the fixture lab, the 300 submissions across correct / partial / malformed / adversarial, and the golden per-student score vectors with a documented byte-identical regeneration command. **No other issue may seed a second corpus.** #697 grades "all 300 fixture submissions" (its AC-1) and its Outcome already refers to "the CAP-21 300-submission fixture corpus"; that referent is this issue.

The reason this matters beyond tidiness: the CAP-21 claim is that four adapters produce byte-identical per-student score vectors. If two adapters measure against two corpora, byte-identity becomes a comparison of apparatuses rather than of adapters, and a genuine adapter divergence can hide inside a fixture divergence. Same constraint already placed on #724 with respect to #524's single seeded violation, for the same reason.

### 2. The missing `blocks` edges

This issue declares `ordering_after: [524, 300]` and no `blocks` at all, so nothing downstream records that it is a prerequisite. It has at least four consumers — one per CAP-21 adapter — of which #697 is the one confirmed by name today.

**Read this issue as carrying `blocks: [697, …the other three adapter corpus-run tasks]`**, with #719 (TASK-C531-2, `CrossPlatformScoreParityTest`) as a transitive consumer downstream of all four rather than a direct one. The chain is: this issue → the four adapter corpus runs → #719's four-way byte-identity assertion.

That also corrects an inversion on the consumer side, recorded there: #697 declares `ordering_after: [..., 531]`, i.e. behind the entire feature — while #719, *inside* #531, consumes #697's output. Ordering behind a feature when the real dependency is one of its tasks turns a clean producer/consumer chain into a cycle. #697 now reads `ordering_after: [717, …]`, `blocks: [719]`.

### 3. One consequence for this task's own AC-4, stated rather than left to be discovered

AC-4 requires the corpus's on-disk size to be stated and the repo's large-fixture policy applied **before it lands**. If that policy forces the corpus smaller than 300, it is not only this issue's acceptance criteria that move: #697 AC-1 asserts the number **300** literally, and #697 AC-2's wall-time budget is derived from the corpus size. Whatever number this issue lands with is the number those criteria take, and the change must be recorded on #697 rather than absorbed silently. Better still, resolve the large-fixture policy question before writing 300 into a third place.

### 4. Not decided here

`ordering_after: [524, 300]` is left as written — #524's frozen CLI contract is what the golden vectors are derived from, which is a real edge. Nothing was merged, nothing closed, no acceptance criterion removed.

**Mirror posted on #697.**

## ADVERSARIAL REVIEW (slice: collab-arch) — AC-1 and AC-2 are already true of master; this task is smaller than it reads

This comment supersedes AC-1, AC-2 and AC-5 as written, and the `band_mw` estimate. The Outcome is otherwise sound.

### 1. AC-2 is shipped, in exactly the form it asks for

AC-2 asks for *"a committed check [that] binds the document to the catalog: a seam added, renamed or removed without a corresponding document change fails the build."*

**That check exists and has existed since PR #259.** At `29afb26`, [`test/jls/ExtensionPointCatalogTest.java`](https://github.com/anadon/JLS/blob/29afb26/test/jls/ExtensionPointCatalogTest.java#L165) carries `docTableAndConstantsAgreeBothWays` — a reflective sweep that collects every `ExtensionPoint` constant in the tree and cross-checks it against the [`docs/extension-points.md`](https://github.com/anadon/JLS/blob/29afb26/docs/extension-points.md) table **in both directions**. The catalog document states the rule normatively: *"adding a typed-now row without a constant, or a constant without a row, is a build failure."* Sibling assertions `contractsAreClosedTypes` and the id-convention checks pin the rest.

**AC-2 is therefore already met and must not be re-implemented.** Restated as AC-2′: *the existing bidirectional check is **extended** to cover the examples AC-3 adds, so an example that stops compiling against a changed seam fails the build alongside the row itself.* That extension is real work; building a second doc/catalog binding is not.

### 2. AC-1 is met except for the examples

The document already lists every catalogued seam with its contract type, home package, cardinality, lifecycle phase and status — seven rows, four typed-now, three `pending` with named owners. What it does **not** carry is a worked example per seam. AC-1′: *each typed-now seam gains one worked example; the enumeration is not re-authored.* This is the same instruction #403 gives in its own method (*"Do not re-author what shipped"*) and the same correction posted on parent #569.

### 3. AC-5's boundary reference is dangling

AC-5 reads *"the single in-tree loading class stays in #399"*. **#399 was closed on 2026-08-08 as `duplicate`, `duplicate_of: 212`**, with its whole content absorbed into [#212](https://github.com/anadon/JLS/issues/212#issuecomment-5227084516) — including the `ForeignElement` design that phrase refers to. Corrected: *the single in-tree loading class stays in **#212***. The other two boundary clauses (catalog mechanics → #223, ServiceLoader mechanism → #212) are unchanged and correct.

### 4. Consequence for cost

With AC-1 reduced to examples and AC-2 reduced to extending a check that already exists, `band_mw: "0.5-1"` is now an over-estimate for what remains. The residual is: worked examples per typed-now seam, their CI compilation (AC-3), the explicit not-an-extension-point section (AC-4), and the extension of `ExtensionPointCatalogTest` to cover them. AC-3 and AC-4 are untouched by this comment and remain the substance of the task.

### 5. One thing this task should not silently inherit

AC-4 asks the document to state *"which seams are not extension points (internal surfaces a plugin must not reach for)"*. Note that three of the seven catalogued rows are `pending` — named seams whose contracts do not yet exist (`hdl.importer` → #61/#62, `app.command` → #84, `gui.theme` → #76). A `pending` row is neither "an extension point a plugin may use" nor "an internal surface"; it is a third state. AC-4 must say which of the three buckets a `pending` row falls into for a reader following this document today, or an outside developer will bind to a row that has no contract.
